title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: Profitability on the income statement is an opinion until working capital and capital expenditure settle the bill on the cash flow statement.
epigraph.author: Credit & Cash Flow Primer

web_blocks.text: Go-To-Market Channels: OEM Direct vs. Trailer Builders & Aftermarket

web_blocks.html: Kross Limited sells through two main channels with very different payment speeds and pricing power. In its core truck and tractor parts line, Kross uses a direct OEM B2B model [1][2]. Engineers co-design parts with Tata Motors, Ashok Leyland, or tractor OEMs, run multi-year durability tests, and ship just-in-time from Jamshedpur [1][2]. Once a part is dual-sourced or single-sourced on a platform, orders track the OEM's monthly build plan with low selling cost.

In trailer axles and suspensions, the buyer base is more spread out. Alongside big trailer OEMs like Tata International DLT, Kross sells to regional trailer builders, fleets, and a growing aftermarket [2][6]. Regional trailer builders are smaller and tighter on cash than listed truck OEMs. As trailer axles grew from 30% to nearly 49% of sales, receivable days rose in step [3][11]. Exports sit near ~8% of the parts unit and run through direct Tier-1 tests in Europe [9]. Those contracts take longer to win, yet offer better margins [9].

web_blocks.text: Jamshedpur Footprint, Backward Integration & Raw Material Pass-Through

web_blocks.html: All five Kross plants sit together in the Adityapur Industrial Area in Gamharia, Jamshedpur [1][2]. Clustering cuts hauling costs as billets move from forging presses to furnaces, CNC cells, and axle bays. Raw steel—alloy bars, billets, and seamless tubes—takes ~54% of sales (₹364.47 Cr Cost of Materials Consumed on ₹673.20 Cr sales in FY26) [10]. OEM contracts pass steel cost changes through with a one-to-two-quarter lag [9]. That protects rupees-per-tonne spreads over time, though sudden steel spikes pinch gross margins for a quarter or two [9].

To capture upstream profit and cut reliance on outside tube mills, Kross built an axle beam extrusion line (at 60%–65% use in FY27) [9][14]. It is also finishing a ₹167 Cr seamless tube plant (~40,000 TPA, 115mm–220mm size) set for trials in February–March 2027 [9][14]. Management targets 300–400 bps of structural EBITDA margin gain once in-house tubes replace bought tubes [14]. Until commercial ramp-up in FY28, however, Kross carries higher depreciation, interest, and stock costs without that margin lift [1][9].

web_blocks.text: Working Capital & Cash Conversion Unit Economics

web_blocks.html: The main drag on Kross's unit economics is working capital. From FY23 to FY26, debtor days nearly tripled from 39 days to 107 days [1]. Inventory days rose from 78 days to 105 days, stretching the cash conversion cycle from 74 days to 153 days [1]. High stock reflects raw steel buffers for forging and finished axle kits waiting for dispatch [1][11]. Meanwhile, 107 debtor days stem from longer credit to trailer builders and OEMs alongside advance payments to steel mills and MSME vendors [1][11].

Every ₹100 of FY26 sales (₹673.0 Cr total) yielded ₹13.08 of operating EBITDA (₹88.0 Cr) [1][10]. Raw materials and stock changes took ₹54.26, employee pay took ₹5.85, and power and plant expenses took ₹26.81 [1][10]. After ₹1.34 of depreciation, ₹1.19 of interest, ₹0.59 of other income, and ₹2.97 of taxes, net profit was ₹8.17 (₹55.0 Cr) per ₹100 of sales [1]. Yet working capital ate over half of that profit, leaving just ₹4.16 of operating cash flow (₹28.0 Cr) per ₹100 of sales [1][11]. Subtracting ₹14.86 of capex (₹100.0 Cr) left negative free cash flow of -₹10.70 per ₹100 of sales (-₹72.0 Cr total) [1][11].

That cash math explains why Kross needed fresh outside funding in 2026. When a firm nets only ₹4.16 of operating cash per ₹100 of sales while spending ₹14.86 on new machines, internal cash cannot pay the bill [1]. As a result, borrowings rose back to ₹119 Cr by September 2026 [1][11]. Kross also raised ₹63.6 Cr via shares and warrants in October 2026 [12]. Cutting debtor days back below 80 days is thus just as vital as winning new orders.

book_paragraphs: How a company sells its product and collects its cash tells you far more about its bargaining power than an investor presentation ever will. At Kross Limited, you and I are looking at two very different commercial worlds operating out of the same Jamshedpur campus.

On the truck and tractor side, Kross sells directly to large OEMs like Ashok Leyland, Tata Motors, and TAFE. The qualification bar is high and the schedule is predictable, but the OEM holds the pricing power and pays on structured corporate terms. Steel price changes pass through with a one-to-two-quarter lag, which protects long-term spreads while compressing margins temporarily when alloy steel rallies. On the trailer axle side, Kross sells both to organized trailer OEMs like Tata International DLT and to smaller regional trailer fabricators across India. Those smaller builders run lean balance sheets and routinely demand extended credit. Meanwhile, large steel mills demand prompt payment for alloy billets. Sitting in the middle of that squeeze is Kross's working capital.

Look at the numbers in our FY26 ₹100 revenue waterfall. Out of every ₹100 Kross billed in FY26 (on ₹673 Cr of total sales), raw materials and inventory adjustments took ₹54.26, employees took ₹5.85, and power, forging consumables, and other operating expenses took ₹26.81. That left ₹13.08 of operating profit—respectable for an Indian auto-ancillary. After ₹1.34 of depreciation, ₹1.19 of interest, ₹0.59 of other income, and ₹2.97 of tax, Kross booked ₹8.17 of net profit.

Now follow that ₹8.17 down to actual cash in the bank. Because debtor days stood at 107 days and inventory days at 105 days, working capital ate up almost half of Kross's earnings, leaving only ₹4.16 of operating cash flow per ₹100 of sales—just ₹28 Cr in total. Against that ₹28 Cr of operating cash, Kross spent ₹100 Cr on capital expenditure—₹14.86 for every ₹100 of sales—building out its extrusion and seamless tube lines. The result was -₹72 Cr of free cash flow.

Management's bet is clear: once the ₹167 Cr seamless tube plant enters trials in February–March 2027 and ramps up in FY28, making tubes in-house should lift operating margins by 300 to 400 basis points. Until that happens, every rupee of revenue growth requires heavy working capital and fresh capital expenditure.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: The Working-Capital Tax on Growth
paragraphs: A business that converts only ₹4.16 of every ₹100 in sales into operating cash flow while spending ₹14.86 on capex cannot self-fund rapid growth.
That arithmetic—not management ambition—explains why Kross's debt rose back to ₹119 Cr by September 2026 and why it issued ₹63.6 Cr of preferential equity and warrants in October 2026.

book_subsections.title: OEM Direct Contracts Versus Trailer Builder Channels
paragraphs: Distribution in auto ancillaries is really a story about who holds the negotiating leverage when invoices come due. When Kross supplies forged shafts and spindles directly to Ashok Leyland or Tata Motors, there are no middlemen taking a cut, and production schedules are tied to the OEM’s assembly-line forecasts. That direct relationship keeps selling expenses low, yet it also means Kross accepts standard OEM payment terms and quarterly price-indexation formulas for steel.

On the trailer axle side, the customer base is much more fragmented—hundreds of regional trailer fabricators and fleet operators across India’s industrial corridors. You might expect fragmented buyers to pay faster than giant truck OEMs, but the working-capital ledger tells the opposite story. As trailer sales surged in FY25 and FY26, Kross extended generous credit and carried heavier finished-goods and raw-material buffers to win market share against entrenched rivals. Debtor days stretched to 107 days and inventory days reached 105 days by March 2026.

book_subsections.title: Reading the ₹100 Revenue Waterfall Without Flinching
paragraphs: Let us trace every ₹100 of FY26 sales (₹673 Cr total) through the shop floor so you see where the cash actually went. Raw steel billets and bought-out components consumed ₹54.26 of every ₹100 billed, employee wages took ₹5.85, and other manufacturing expenses—power for induction furnaces, dies, consumables, and freight—absorbed ₹26.81. That left ₹13.08 of operating profit before depreciation, or ₹8.17 of net profit after depreciation, interest, and taxes.

Here is the punchline that separates accounting profit from cash reality: out of that ₹8.17 of net profit, working-capital absorption swallowed most of the cash, leaving just ₹4.16 of operating cash flow per ₹100 of sales. Meanwhile, Kross spent ₹14.86 per ₹100 of sales on capital expenditure to build its extrusion and seamless tube lines, resulting in -₹10.70 of free cash flow per ₹100 of revenue. That cash gap explains why management is betting so heavily on the ₹167 Cr seamless tube plant to cut raw-material dependence by 300 to 400 basis points—and why we must test Kross’s competitive moat next.

Ask yourself what happens if freight rates soften for two quarters while Kross is carrying 105 days of steel inventory and 107 days of customer receivables. Working capital does not automatically shrink on command; instead, slower collections force the company to draw down bank lines just to keep furnaces running. That is why every rupee of margin expansion from the seamless tube plant will only matter if management pairs it with tighter credit discipline on trailer-builder accounts.

Walk through the shop-floor cash cycle one more time, because it is the single most important operational lesson in this entire book. When Kross bills ₹100 of revenue in FY26, ₹54.26 immediately leaves the building to pay for alloy steel billets and bought-out components. Another ₹32.66 pays factory labor, furnace power, dies, and freight. After depreciation, interest, and taxes, ₹8.17 remains as accounting net profit.

If customers paid in 45 days and inventory turned every 45 days, most of that ₹8.17 would land in the bank as cash. Instead, 107 debtor days and 105 inventory days absorbed almost half of it, leaving just ₹4.16 of operating cash flow while capex consumed ₹14.86. That is why vertical integration into seamless tubes—targeted to shave 300 to 400 basis points off raw-material costs—is both Kross’s biggest opportunity and its biggest execution test.

Think about why working capital is the silent governor on Kross’s growth speed. When sales jump 80% in a single quarter—as they did in Q2 FY27—steel billets must be bought months in advance, and trailer fabricators often stretch payment terms.

Unless receivables and inventory turn faster, rapid top-line growth actually drains cash rather than generating it—which is why the ₹100 revenue waterfall in Chapter 3 is your most reliable reality check.

That is why our ₹100 revenue waterfall is the single clearest lens on Kross’s unit economics: until debtor days and inventory days compress from 107 and 105 days respectively, rapid sales growth will continue to consume cash.
